title: August 2026 Security Vulnerability: What happened?
excerpt: Explanation of the August 2026 Security Vulnerability.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
A security issue affecting self-hosted instances was reported, confirmed and patched. This is an account of what happened, what was exposed, and what we changed afterwards.

## What happened

The issue allowed a request to reach an internal endpoint that should have required authentication. It was reported through our disclosure process and confirmed the same day.

## What we did

Patches shipped across every supported version before this was published. Cloud instances were updated first and required no action from customers.

## What changed afterwards

Two things. The endpoint class involved is now covered by a test that asserts authentication rather than assuming it, and our disclosure process now publishes a timeline alongside the fix rather than weeks later.

If you self-host and have not upgraded, that is the one action worth taking today.

title: Join us for AI Analytics Week
excerpt: Three live sessions, August 25–27, on how AI is changing analytics work, how you can keep up, and a 2-minute quiz to figure out which session is best for you.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
Three live sessions on how AI is changing analytics work — what it genuinely helps with, what it quietly makes worse, and how to tell which is which in your own setup.

## The sessions

- **Where agents actually help.** The tasks where a model earns its place, and the ones where it adds a confident wrong answer.
- **On your own infrastructure.** Running analytics agents without sending your warehouse to someone else's API.
- **Verification.** Why an answer you cannot inspect is a rumour with a chart attached.

## Who should come

If you are being asked to "add AI" to your analytics stack and are not sure what that means in practice, the first session is the useful one. If you have already tried and found the results uneven, the third.

All three are recorded and available afterwards without registration.

title: Security-focused Metabase Release Announcement
excerpt: Following our security update last week, today we are releasing hardened versions of Metabase which incorporate several security improvements.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
Following last week's security update, today we are releasing hardened versions that incorporate several improvements beyond the original fix.

## What is in it

The original patch closed the specific issue. This release addresses the surrounding class of problem: tighter defaults on internal endpoints, stricter validation on a handful of request paths, and better logging of authentication failures so that unusual activity is visible rather than silent.

## Upgrading

These are drop-in patch releases for every supported version. No migration, no configuration change.

If you upgraded last week you are not exposed to the original issue, but upgrading again is still worth doing — the hardening here is the part that reduces the chance of a similar report next time.

title: Security update available for Metabase - Please upgrade now
excerpt: We've patched a critical vulnerability.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
A security update is available for all supported versions. If you self-host, upgrading is the recommended action.

## What to do

Upgrade to the latest patch release of whichever major version you run. Metabase Cloud instances have already been updated and require no action.

## If you cannot upgrade immediately

Restricting network access to your instance — putting it behind a VPN or an allowlist rather than exposing it to the public internet — meaningfully reduces exposure in the interim. This is good practice regardless.

A fuller account will follow once deployments have had time to update.

title: How we picked LibreChat — and ended up with a Slack agent
excerpt: How Metabase's Cloud team consolidated AI tooling behind self-hosted LibreChat, contributed upstream MCP fixes, and built LibreBot — a Slack agent for internal tools.
author: Arkadi Yaroslavtsev
body:
We wanted an internal chat interface over our own models and data. We evaluated the self-hosted options, picked LibreChat, and then ended up using something else entirely for most of the actual work.

## Why self-hosted

The requirement was that internal conversations containing customer data should not leave infrastructure we control. That rules out most hosted options immediately and makes the shortlist short.

## What LibreChat gets right

It is genuinely good: multi-model, sensible auth, active development, and it does not try to be a platform. Setup was an afternoon.

## Why we mostly use a Slack agent instead

Because people were already in Slack. The web interface was better in every respect except the one that mattered — whether anyone opened it. Moving the same capability into a Slack agent took usage from a handful of people to most of the company.

The lesson is not about LibreChat. It is that an internal tool competes with the tabs people already have open.

title: Metabase alternatives: comparing platforms for AI analytics
excerpt: How Metabase stacks up against Tableau, Power BI, Looker, Cognos, Hex, Lightdash, Omni, and Superset on AI analytics, pricing, and ease of use in 2026.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
An honest comparison of how Metabase sits against other analytics platforms on AI features, pricing and how quickly a non-specialist can get somewhere useful.

## What actually differentiates platforms now

Every vendor ships natural-language querying. The differentiator is no longer whether a model can write a query — it is whether the answer is traceable to definitions someone has agreed on, and whether you can see the query that produced it.

## Where to look when comparing

- **Can you inspect the query behind an AI answer?** If not, you cannot debug a wrong one.
- **Is the semantic layer a first-class thing or a configuration file?**
- **What does it cost at the point where you want everyone to have access?** Per-seat pricing quietly caps adoption.
- **How long until a non-technical colleague answers their own question?**

## Being fair about it

There are cases where another tool is the better choice — deep statistical work, or an organisation already standardised on a stack. The comparison worth making is against your own constraints, not a feature grid.

title: PA: a persistent agent for developer workflow automation
excerpt: We built a lightweight CLI agent system that automates boring developer tasks and gives back about 15% of the day.
author: Filipe Silva
body:
An experiment in giving an agent continuity across sessions, so that it accumulates context about a codebase rather than starting cold every time.

## The problem with stateless

A fresh agent re-derives the same things every session: where the tests live, which module owns what, which patterns the codebase actually uses versus the ones it used to. That rediscovery is most of the cost and all of the frustration.

## What we built

A long-running process that maintains notes about the repository between invocations, updates them as the code changes, and brings the relevant ones into context when a task starts.

## What it changed

Tasks that previously needed a paragraph of orientation now need a sentence. The agent stops suggesting patterns we abandoned two years ago.

## What it did not fix

Stale notes are worse than no notes. Most of the engineering went into expiring and re-verifying what it thinks it knows, not into storing more.

title: Introducing the Claude skill for learning Metabase
excerpt: Use Claude to teach you Metabase in a structured way, using your own data.
author: Robert Kosara
body:
A packaged skill that teaches Claude how to use Metabase — so that asking it for help with a query or a dashboard produces advice grounded in how the product actually works.

## Why a skill rather than documentation

Models already have some knowledge of Metabase, assembled from whatever was public at training time. That knowledge is uneven and frequently out of date. A skill gives it current, structured material to work from.

## What it covers

The query builder, models, dashboard filters, permissions, and the places where people most reliably get stuck — field filters, linked filters, and the difference between a model and a saved question.

## Using it

Install it and ask ordinary questions. The difference shows up most on the tasks where general knowledge produces plausible but wrong answers.

title: AI for everyone, with confidence
excerpt: We've shipped a lot of AI features since the start of 2026. Here's how they fit together, and why the infrastructure around AI matters as much as the features themselves.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
AI features are now available on every plan, including the free one. The reason that is possible is the same reason they are useful: they are grounded in your semantic layer rather than guessing at your schema.

## What you can do

Ask a question in plain language and get a chart. Click into the chart to find out why. Inspect the query it generated, and change it if it is not what you meant.

## Why the last part matters most

An analytics answer you cannot verify is not an answer, it is a suggestion with a confident tone. Every result shows the query behind it and the definitions it used.

## Grounded, not guessing

When your data team marks a table as canonical and defines a metric, the model uses those rather than inferring intent from column names. That is the difference between a demo and something you would let someone run a board report from.

title: Metabase + OpenAI Codex
excerpt: Metabase is now available as a plugin in ChatGPT Codex, part of OpenAI's new data analytics launch
author: Vamsi Peri
body:
Metabase now works with OpenAI Codex, so you can query and explore your data from inside the environment you are already coding in.

## What it does

It exposes your Metabase instance as a tool: list databases, inspect models, run a question, get results back. The agent works against your governed semantic layer rather than raw tables.

## Permissions

Access follows the permissions of the account the connection is made with. An agent cannot see anything you could not see yourself, which is the only sane default.

## Getting started

Connect your instance and ask. The most useful first task is usually asking what data is available — the answer tends to be more organised than people expect.

title: Welcome to the strip mining era of open source security
excerpt: In 2026, LLM-powered code scanners are uncovering security vulnerabilities in open source projects at 10x the historical rate. Here's what OSS maintainers and users need to do about it.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
Automated vulnerability reporting has industrialised. For maintainers, the result is a steady stream of low-quality reports that cost real time to triage and produce almost nothing.

## What changed

Scanning a public repository and filing a report is now nearly free. Some of that is genuinely useful. Much of it is pattern-matched output filed in volume by people hoping something sticks.

## The cost lands on maintainers

Every report has to be read, because the one you dismiss is the one that was real. That asymmetry is the whole problem: the reporter spends seconds, the maintainer spends an hour.

## What helps

- Requiring a working reproduction, not a scanner excerpt
- Publishing clearly what is and is not in scope
- Being willing to close reports without a reproduction, politely and quickly

None of this is hostile to security research. Good researchers already do these things, and they are the ones currently drowned out.

title: Winners of the Metabase AI Hackathon
excerpt: See what two developers built with the Metabase MCP server and file-based development — and why we picked them as our AI Hackathon winners.
author: Ramiro Nunez Dosio
body:
The results from our AI hackathon, where the brief was deliberately open: build something with Metabase and a model that you would actually use.

## What won

The standout projects shared a pattern — none of them were chat interfaces. The winners used models for narrow, well-defined jobs inside an existing workflow: classifying incoming support tickets into dashboard dimensions, generating documentation for undocumented tables, and flagging dashboards whose underlying queries had silently started returning zero rows.

## What we learned

The projects that impressed were the ones where the model did something specific and the human stayed in the loop. The general-purpose assistants were uniformly less convincing than their demos suggested.

Thank you to everyone who entered. The submissions are public and worth browsing.

title: Improving the performance of the popular Clojure development tool clojure-lsp
excerpt: Have you found clojure-lsp struggling with your large codebase? We did, so we made some improvements to our favorite development tool to cut startup time in half and memory allocation by two thirds.
author: Sashko Yakushev
body:
We depend on clojure-lsp daily, and on a codebase our size it had become slow enough to be disruptive. Here is what we found and what we changed upstream.

## Profiling first

The bottleneck was not where anyone guessed. Most of the time went into repeated analysis of unchanged namespaces during incremental updates — work that was already done and immediately discarded.

## The changes

Caching analysis results keyed on file content, short-circuiting the dependency walk when nothing downstream changed, and avoiding a serialisation round-trip that was happening on every keystroke in large files.

## The result

Completion latency on our codebase dropped substantially, and the editor stopped pausing on save.

## Upstreaming

All of it went upstream. The maintainers were generous with review, and the changes benefit anyone working on a large Clojure project, not just us.

title: How we built ten custom subagents to tame a 500K-line Clojure codebase
excerpt: We built ten domain-expert subagents to manage context when working on Metabase's 500K+ line backend.
author: Bryan Maass
body:
Our codebase is around half a million lines of Clojure. Generic coding agents struggle with it, so we built ten narrow ones instead.

## Why narrow

A general agent asked to change something in a codebase this size spends most of its effort orienting, and orients wrongly often enough to be unreliable. Agents scoped to one concern — the query processor, the driver layer, the frontend state — carry the right context from the start.

## The ten

They cover areas with distinct conventions: database drivers, the query processor, permissions, the embedding SDK, migrations, tests, and a few more. Each knows its area's patterns and, importantly, its area's traps.

## What worked

The specialised agents are dramatically more useful on their own turf. The honest caveat is that routing a task to the right one is still a human judgement, and tasks that span two areas remain hard.

## What we would do differently

We over-invested in the agents and under-invested in the routing. That is where the remaining friction is.

title: Metabase AI Hackathon
excerpt: Build anything with Metabase MCP and AI tools and get the chance to win mechanical keyboards
author: Ramiro Nunez Dosio
body:
We are running a hackathon. The brief is open: build something using Metabase and a language model that you would genuinely use afterwards.

## What we are looking for

Not chat interfaces. We have seen a lot of chat interfaces. The interesting submissions tend to be narrow — a model doing one specific job inside a workflow that already exists.

## Rules

Any language, any model, anything that touches Metabase. Teams up to four. Submit a repository and a short video showing it working.

## Judging

Usefulness first, then originality, then execution. A rough prototype of something people want beats a polished version of something nobody asked for.

title: Meet Repro-Bot, our GitHub issue triage agent
excerpt: Repro-Bot is an AI agent that reproduces issues in the Metabase backlog to help us fix bugs faster.
author: Nathan Voxland
body:
Repro-Bot reads new GitHub issues, tries to reproduce them against a clean instance, and comments with what it found.

## Why reproduction specifically

Most open-source bug reports are missing the one detail that would make them actionable. Someone has to ask for it, and that someone burns out. Reproduction is a bounded, mechanical task — exactly the kind a machine should take.

## What it does well

Around a third of reports reproduce cleanly. For those it attaches a stack trace and the version where behaviour changed, turning a multi-day exchange into one comment a maintainer can act on.

## Where it fails

Environment-specific problems. Anything involving a database driver, a proxy or a particular SSO setup produced confident nonsense. It now refuses rather than speculates.

## One rule we got wrong first

We let it close issues it could not reproduce. That was a mistake — those reports were disproportionately the hardest and most valuable. It escalates now.

title: Meet Data Studio: tools to curate your semantic layer in Metabase
excerpt: An analyst workbench with tools for shaping data and curating your semantic layer in Metabase.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
Data Studio is a workbench for shaping data and curating the semantic layer — the place where raw tables become things with agreed meanings.

## What it is for

Marking which tables are canonical and which are somebody's scratch work. Defining metrics once, so that "active customer" means the same thing in two different dashboards. Documenting the joins that are legitimate and the ones that silently multiply your rows.

## Why now

Because agents made it urgent. When people wrote every query by hand, tribal knowledge about which table to use was slow but survivable. When a model composes a query in seconds, the absence of a stated definition means it guesses.

## For analysts

It is a workbench, not a config file. Shape data, preview results, and promote something to canonical when you are confident in it.

title: February 2026 vulnerability: What happened?
excerpt: A recap of the notifications endpoint vulnerability and our response.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
An account of the February 2026 vulnerability: the timeline, what was affected, and what we have changed.

## Timeline

Reported through our disclosure process, confirmed within hours, patched across supported versions, and published once deployments had time to update.

## What was affected

Self-hosted instances on the affected versions. Cloud instances were patched before disclosure.

## What we changed

The specific fix matters less than the surrounding changes: additional test coverage for the class of issue, tighter defaults, and a faster path from report to confirmed triage.

## What you should do

If you self-host and have not upgraded, do that. If you have, there is nothing further required.

title: Security update available for Metabase - Please upgrade now
excerpt: We've patched a severe vulnerability uncovered by a third-party security researcher.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
A security update is available. Self-hosted instances should upgrade promptly.

## What to do

Upgrade to the latest patch of your major version. Cloud instances are already updated.

## Reducing exposure in the meantime

If an immediate upgrade is not possible, restrict network access to the instance. Analytics tools rarely need to be reachable from the public internet, and putting one behind a VPN is worth doing permanently.

A post-mortem will follow.

title: Lessons learned from building AI analytics agents: build for chaos
excerpt: A production disaster taught us a lot about building AI analytics agents. Learn why context engineering beats prompts and why you should build for chaos.
author: Thomas Schmidt
body:
We have been building analytics agents for a while now. The main lesson is that the demo path is narrow and reality is not.

## Build for chaos

Real schemas have columns named `status_2`, tables nobody can explain, and three date fields where only one is correct. An agent tuned on a clean schema falls apart immediately.

## What actually helped

- **Refuse rather than guess.** An agent that says it cannot answer is more useful than one that produces a plausible wrong number.
- **Ground everything in definitions.** If a metric is defined, use it. If it is not, say so rather than inventing one.
- **Show the query.** Every answer carries its SQL. This single thing did more for trust than any accuracy improvement.
- **Expect follow-ups.** The first question is rarely the real question.

## The uncomfortable finding

Accuracy improvements mattered less than transparency improvements. People tolerated a wrong answer they could see and correct far better than a right answer they had to take on faith.

title: We simplified embedding
excerpt: We cleaned up how embedding works in Metabase. Two paths: modular embedding for individual components, or full-app embedding for the whole thing. Your existing embeds still work.
author: Jeff Bruemmer
body:
Embedding used to require choosing between three approaches with overlapping names and different trade-offs. We have simplified it.

## What changed

One path to get started, which scales up rather than forcing a migration later. Begin with a dashboard in an iframe; move to the SDK when you need component-level control; add interactivity without rebuilding.

## The naming

The old names described implementation rather than intent, which made the documentation hard to navigate. The new terms describe what you get.

## Migrating

Existing embeds keep working. There is no forced migration — the simplification is about new setups and about making the upgrade path obvious when you outgrow where you started.

title: Become a data analyst in 2026: a practical roadmap
excerpt: Thinking of becoming a data analyst in 2026? This roadmap covers the essentials to get started with confidence.
author: Abed Habli
body:
A practical roadmap for becoming a data analyst, written to be followed rather than admired.

## Start with SQL

Not a course. Get access to a real dataset and answer real questions badly until you answer them well. Joins, aggregation and window functions cover most working analysis.

## Then a visualisation tool

Learn one properly rather than three superficially. The skill that transfers is knowing which chart answers which question.

## Then the part nobody lists

Learn to interrogate a request. Most analyst work is translating a vague question into a specific one, and the translation is where the value is. A technically perfect answer to the wrong question is worthless.

## What to skip early

Machine learning, until you can reliably produce a correct weekly report. Almost nobody is blocked on modelling; most are blocked on definitions.

## Building a portfolio

One analysis of a dataset you find genuinely interesting, written up with the reasoning visible, beats five tutorial notebooks.

title: 10 B2B SaaS product metrics that should be on your dashboard
excerpt: A guide to key SaaS product metrics - from website-to-signup and activation rates to churn and NDR
author: Tanya Aulachynskaya
body:
Ten metrics worth having on a B2B SaaS dashboard, and a note on why most dashboards have the wrong ten.

## The list

- **Activation rate** — share of signups reaching the value moment
- **Net revenue retention** — expansion minus contraction on existing accounts
- **Logo churn** — customers lost, regardless of size
- **Time to first value** — signup to the moment the product does something useful
- **Weekly active accounts** — accounts, not users
- **Expansion revenue** — growth from existing customers
- **CAC payback** — months to recover acquisition cost
- **Feature adoption depth** — how many core features an account actually uses
- **Support ticket rate per account** — a leading indicator of churn
- **Pipeline-to-close rate** — by source

## Why most dashboards have the wrong ten

They track what is easy to measure rather than what predicts anything. Pageviews are easy. Activation is hard and tells you whether next quarter happens.

## The definitions matter more than the list

Every one of these hides a decision. Writing the definition next to the number is the difference between a dashboard and an argument.

title: Metabase Community Data Stack Report 2025
excerpt: We asked 330+ teams how they build and use their data stacks - from tool choices to AI adoption. Here's what we learned.
author: Alex Yarosh
body:
Results from this year's community data stack survey — what data teams are actually running, as opposed to what conference talks suggest.

## The headline

Stacks are smaller than the discourse implies. The median respondent runs a warehouse, a transformation tool and a BI tool. The elaborate multi-layer architectures are a minority.

## Warehouses

Postgres remains extremely common, including at organisations large enough to have moved on. "We never needed to migrate" came up repeatedly.

## Where time goes

Respondents consistently reported that most effort goes into definitions and data quality, not tooling. The tools are not the bottleneck and have not been for some time.

## AI

Widely experimented with, narrowly deployed. The most common production use was documentation and classification rather than query generation.

title: The story behind our AI Dataset Generator
excerpt: Explore the design choices, challenges, and achievements behind our open source AI Dataset Generator.
author: Matthew Hefferon
body:
We needed realistic sample data for demos and testing. Here is why generating it turned out to be harder than it sounds.

## Why not real data

Obvious reasons. Why not random data? Because random data has no structure, and analytics on structureless data produces flat lines and meaningless correlations. Demos fall apart.

## What realistic means

Seasonality. Weekday and weekend differences. Cohorts that behave differently. Occasional anomalies worth finding. Referential integrity that holds up under joins.

## The approach

Generate from a model of the business rather than from distributions — simulate customers signing up, using the product, upgrading and churning, then derive the tables from the simulation. The patterns emerge because the underlying behaviour produced them.

## The surprise

The hardest part was making anomalies that were interesting but not obvious. Too subtle and nobody finds them; too blunt and the exercise is trivial.

title: How to build sales dashboards that sales teams actually use
excerpt: Build a sales dashboard your team will actually use. See 10 key metrics, tips, and a live example in Metabase.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Sales dashboards have a high build rate and a low usage rate. The reason is usually that they were designed for the person who requested them rather than the people who open them.

## Start from the meeting

If there is a weekly pipeline review, build the dashboard that meeting needs — in the order the meeting goes through things. A dashboard that matches an existing ritual gets used. One that requires a new ritual does not.

## What belongs on it

- Pipeline by stage, with movement since last week
- Deals that have not moved, which is the most actionable thing on the page
- Forecast against target
- Activity, only if someone will act on it

## What to leave off

Anything nobody can act on by Friday. Historical trend charts belong in a separate monthly view.

## Make the owner obvious

Put a name on it. Dashboards without an owner become untrustworthy within two quarters, and nobody can say when it happened.

title: What is embedded analytics?
excerpt: Embedded analytics means giving your users access to charts, metrics, and reports directly inside your product, so they can explore and act on their data without needing to leave your app or rely on someone else for answers.
author: Alex Yarosh
body:
Embedded analytics means putting reporting inside your own product, so your customers see data about their own usage without leaving it.

## The distinction that matters

Internal BI serves your team and can assume context. Embedded analytics serves your customers, who have none — which means it has to be self-explanatory, correctly scoped, and good enough to sit next to the rest of your product.

## What it requires

- **Tenant isolation.** Each customer sees only their own rows, enforced at the data layer rather than in application code.
- **Styling control.** It should look like your product.
- **Performance under concurrency.** Every customer hitting it at once is the normal case.

## Build or embed

A charting library is the easy part. The query layer, permissions, caching and the long tail of expected interactions are where the quarters go.

title: The Metabase Community Data Stack Survey: by data teams, for data teams
excerpt: How the modern data stack is evolving: share yours and see how it compares
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
We are running the community data stack survey again. It takes a few minutes and the results are published openly.

## Why bother

Most published information about what data teams use comes from vendors with something to sell. This is an attempt at something less self-interested — what people actually run, including the unfashionable parts.

## What we ask

Warehouse, transformation, orchestration, BI, team size, and where your time actually goes. Nothing identifying.

## What happens to it

Aggregated, analysed and published, including the findings that are inconvenient for us.

title: Top 5 Dashboard fails (and how to fix them)
excerpt: Dashboards are meant to guide decisions, not create confusion. In this guide, we’ll walk through five common pitfalls and how to fix them.
author: Abed Habli
body:
Five failure modes that show up repeatedly, and what to do instead.

## 1. Too many questions on one screen

A dashboard answering one question with three charts outperforms one answering nine with twenty. Split it.

## 2. No stated question

If the title is "Overview", nobody knows what it is for, including the person who built it.

## 3. Numbers without definitions

Two dashboards showing different revenue figures destroy trust in both. Put the definition next to the number.

## 4. No owner

Unowned dashboards decay silently. Someone has to be responsible for whether it is still correct.

## 5. Built for the requester, not the reader

The executive who asked for it is not the person opening it daily. Design for the latter.

## The pattern underneath

Every one of these is a communication failure rather than a technical one, which is why adding more charts never fixes them.

title: Introducing Metabase's new Embedded Analytics SDK for React
excerpt: The React toolkit for custom embedded analytics that integrates seamlessly in your UI
author: Jess Thompson
body:
The Embedded Analytics SDK lets you drop Metabase components into a React application and style them as your own.

## What it gives you

Component-level control rather than an iframe. Render a single question, an interactive query builder, or a full dashboard, and pass your own theme.

## Authentication

It plugs into your existing auth. Your app signs a token, the SDK uses it, and permissions follow from there — including row-level scoping per tenant.

## When to use it over an iframe

When you need the analytics to feel like part of the product rather than a window into another one: your fonts, your colours, your layout, your loading states.

## Getting started

Install the package, configure the provider with your instance URL and auth endpoint, and render a component.

title: Maps data visualizations: best practices
excerpt: Learn how to create impactful map data visualizations with tips on using pin maps, grid maps, and region maps to highlight patterns and make data-driven decisions.
author: Alex Yarosh
body:
Maps are the most over-used chart type in analytics, because geography is usually a grouping dimension rather than the point.

## When a map earns its place

When position itself carries meaning — delivery routes, store catchments, regional coverage gaps. If you are comparing values across regions, a sorted bar chart does it better and in less space.

## Choosing a type

- **Choropleth** for rates normalised by population or area. Never for raw counts, which just show you where people live.
- **Pin map** for individual locations, up to a few hundred.
- **Heat map** for density, when individual points stop being distinguishable.

## The normalisation trap

A choropleth of raw totals is a population map with extra steps. Divide by something.

title: How to visualize time-series data: best practices
excerpt: Learn about time-series data and how to visualize it. With best practices and a handy cheat sheet.
author: Alex Yarosh
body:
Time series looks like the easy case and quietly is not.

## Start with the axis

A truncated y-axis makes noise look like a trend. For time series, start at zero unless you have a specific reason, and say so when you do not.

## Match granularity to the question

Daily data over two years is unreadable. Weekly or monthly aggregation reveals the trend the daily view hides. Keep the daily view available for drilling.

## Seasonality

Most business metrics have a weekly cycle. Comparing Monday to Sunday is meaningless; comparing this Monday to last Monday is not. Period-over-period comparison beats a raw line for anything with a cycle.

## Annotate

The spike in March has an explanation. Putting it on the chart saves everyone the meeting.

title: How to build better line and bar charts
excerpt: Learn how to improve bar and line charts by choosing the right type, reducing clutter, and highlighting data. More best practices and a handy cheat sheet.
author: Alex Yarosh
body:
Most charts are line or bar charts, which means most chart improvements are improvements to these two.

## Bar charts

Sort by value, not alphabetically, unless the categories have an inherent order. Start the axis at zero — truncating a bar axis is actively misleading because bar length is the encoding.

## Line charts

Three or four lines is the practical limit before the legend becomes a lookup exercise. Past that, use small multiples.

## Both

- Label directly instead of using a legend where you can
- Use colour to mean something, not to decorate
- Keep gridlines faint
- Round the axis labels; nobody needs four decimal places

## The test

Show it to someone who was not in the meeting. If they need a sentence of explanation, the chart has not done its job.

title: How we enriched customer contact and organization data
excerpt: To improve self-service at Metabase, we used open-source tools like dlt to automate contact enrichment and tailor data models for different teams.
author: Max Zheng
body:
An account of cleaning up our own contact and organisation data, which was worse than we expected.

## The problem

The same organisation existed several times under different spellings. Personal and work emails for the same person were unlinked. Nobody could answer how many organisations we actually talked to.

## What we did

Normalised domains first, which collapsed a surprising share of the duplicates immediately. Then matched on domain, then fuzzy-matched names within a domain, reviewing anything below a confidence threshold by hand.

## What we learned

The automated passes handled the bulk and the remainder was genuinely ambiguous — subsidiaries, rebrands, consultants with several clients. Those need a human and a documented rule, not a better algorithm.

## Keeping it clean

The cleanup is worthless without a constraint at the point of entry. We added one.

title: Set up a basic pipeline for log analysis
excerpt: You can use a BI tool for small scale log analysis with data visualizations. Here are a few tips and suggestions to get started.
author: Tanya Aulachynskaya
body:
A basic pipeline for getting application logs somewhere you can query them, without adopting an observability platform.

## The shape

Structured logs to a file or stream, batched into a table in your warehouse, queried like anything else. For many teams this is sufficient and costs almost nothing.

## Structure the logs first

JSON lines with consistent field names. Parsing unstructured text later is miserable and lossy; a small amount of discipline at write time saves all of it.

## What to keep

Timestamp, level, service, request id, user id where lawful, duration, outcome. Request id is the one people forget and the one that makes tracing possible.

## Retention

Decide up front. Logs grow faster than anything else in the warehouse, and a table nobody pruned is how surprise bills happen.

title: Embed a Metabase dashboard in Zendesk
excerpt: Get the customer data and insights you need automatically filtered and ready for use within your support tickets. You can also embed a dashboard in Salesforce, Stripe, Jira, or platforms that allow embedding URLs.
author: Ignacio Beines Furcada
body:
Putting a dashboard inside Zendesk so support agents see account context without switching tabs.

## Why it helps

Agents answering a ticket need the account's usage, plan and recent errors. Every tab switch is friction, and friction at scale means it does not happen.

## The approach

A Zendesk app rendering an embedded dashboard, parameterised by the ticket's organisation id so it scopes to the right account automatically.

## Scoping

The organisation id comes from the ticket context and is passed as a locked parameter — the agent cannot change it, which keeps the view correct and the permissions honest.

## What to put on it

Less than you think. Plan, usage trend, recent errors, open tickets. Anything more and agents stop reading it.

title: Keeping tabs on embedded analytics
excerpt: Metabase's usage analytics can help you learn who your most engaged customers are and what’s most important to them.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
If you have embedded analytics in your product, you should know which parts customers actually use.

## Why

Embedded dashboards accumulate the same way internal ones do. Without usage data you cannot tell which are load-bearing and which are costing you query time for nobody.

## What to track

Views per dashboard per tenant, which cards get interacted with, and which filters get changed. The last one is the most informative — a filter nobody touches is a default that should be the only option.

## Acting on it

Retire what nobody opens. Promote what everyone does. If one tenant uses something heavily and nobody else does, that is a conversation about either a feature or a bespoke report.

title: Comparing the most popular open-source charting libraries
excerpt: Discover features from commonly used data visualization libraries, like Chart.js, ECharts, and Nivo.
author: Matthew Hefferon
body:
A comparison of the main open-source charting libraries, from the perspective of building an analytics product rather than a one-off visualisation.

## What matters at this scale

- **Bundle size**, because it ships to every user on every page
- **Accessibility**, which most libraries treat as optional
- **Interaction model**, specifically whether you can hook into clicks for drill-down
- **Rendering strategy** — SVG is easier to style and slower past a few thousand points

## The trade-off

Low-level libraries give control and cost you months. High-level ones get you running in a day and fight you on the eleventh customisation. Which is right depends on whether charts are your product or part of it.

## A note on performance

Most libraries are fine until a few thousand points. If you routinely exceed that, canvas rendering is not optional and that narrows the field considerably.

title: Understand how your team uses Metabase
excerpt: Learn which dashboards are most popular, how to track active users and changes to settings and configurations, view audit logs to monitor incidents, and more.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
Usage analytics shows you how your organisation actually uses its own instance.

## The questions it answers

Which dashboards get opened, by how many distinct people, and which have not been touched this quarter. Who is querying, and whether that is spreading beyond the data team.

## The first thing to look at

Distinct viewers per dashboard over ninety days. The distribution is usually steeper than anyone expects — a handful carry everything, and a long tail carries nobody.

## Acting on it

Archive the tail. It is recoverable and nobody will notice. Then put owners on the survivors.

## The adoption question

Track distinct queriers outside the data team over time. That single number tells you whether self-service is real or aspirational.

title: Metabase housekeeping with usage analytics
excerpt: Clear out outdated, unused questions and dashboards to make space for the most valuable stuff. Improve load times by caching the questions that consume the most resources.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
A practical routine for keeping an instance tidy, using usage data rather than opinion.

## Quarterly, in order

1. **Archive dashboards with no views in ninety days.** Recoverable, uncontroversial, and it removes most of the clutter.
2. **Find duplicate names.** Six dashboards called some variant of "Revenue" is why people ask an analyst instead of searching.
3. **Check ownership.** Anything without a current owner either gets one or gets archived.
4. **Review expensive queries.** A handful of dashboards usually account for most of the warehouse cost.

## Why it decays

Nothing is wrong with creating dashboards freely. The failure is never retiring them, which is a process gap rather than a tooling one.

## Make it someone's job

An hour a quarter, on a recurring invite. Otherwise it does not happen.

title: How data-driven is your org?
excerpt: How to take usage analytics to organize your Metabase and point people to the data they want to (and should be) looking at.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
A way of asking how data-driven your organisation actually is, using evidence rather than self-assessment.

## The metric that matters

Distinct people outside the data team who ran a query this month. Not dashboard views — views are passive and can be a screen in a corridor. Queries mean someone had a question and pursued it.

## What good looks like

The number grows, and it grows outside the functions you would expect. Finance and product adopting analytics is normal; support and operations adopting it is the signal that something has genuinely changed.

## The counter-indicator

If dashboard views are high and distinct queriers are flat, you have a reporting culture rather than an analytical one. People are reading what they are given and not asking anything of their own.

title: 10 handy Metabase features you may not know about
excerpt: Here are ten features of Metabase that may take some time to discover, but once you do you may find yourself using all the time.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
Ten things that exist, that people routinely do not know exist.

## The list

- **Click behaviour on dashboard cards** — send a click to another dashboard, a URL, or a filtered view
- **Linked filters**, so choosing a country narrows the city list
- **SQL snippets** for logic you paste into every query
- **Field filters**, which make SQL questions work with dashboard filters properly
- **Models** as a reusable starting point rather than copying a question
- **Alerts** on a result crossing a threshold
- **Dashboard subscriptions** delivering results by email or Slack on a schedule
- **Public links** for sharing with people who have no account
- **Keyboard shortcuts** — press `?` to see them
- **Converting a question to SQL** to see exactly what the builder generated

## The last one

It is the best way to learn what the query builder is doing, and the fastest way to settle an argument about whether a result is right.

title: Choose where your Metabase Cloud is hosted
excerpt: Speed up your Metabase by hosting it closer to you and your data with new cloud-hosting options in the EU (Frankfurt), APAC (Singapore, Sydney), or South America (São Paulo).
author: Jess Thompson
body:
You can now choose the region your Metabase Cloud instance runs in.

## Why it matters

Two reasons. Data residency requirements that specify where data is processed, and latency — an instance close to your warehouse is noticeably faster, because the round trip happens on every query.

## Choosing

Pick the region closest to your warehouse rather than closest to your office. Query latency dominates; interface latency is barely perceptible by comparison.

## Changing later

Possible, but it involves a migration. Worth getting right at setup.

title: Vulnerability post-mortem: July 2023
excerpt: A recap of the H2 Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability and our response.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
An account of the July 2023 vulnerability, what was affected and what changed afterwards.

## What happened

An issue in a component reachable before authentication. Reported responsibly, confirmed quickly, patched across supported versions.

## Who was affected

Self-hosted instances on affected versions, particularly those exposed directly to the internet. Cloud instances were patched before disclosure.

## What we changed

Additional review of pre-authentication code paths, which are now treated as a distinct risk category with their own test requirements.

## The general lesson

Analytics tools rarely need to be publicly reachable. Putting yours behind a VPN limits the blast radius of a whole class of issue, including ones not yet found.

title: Advice for building and scaling an effective and happy data team
excerpt: If you don't understand data roles enough to scope job descriptions or workload, get ready for burnout, turnover, and the death of company-wide data culture. Our data team offers some advice on how to build a healthy data team.
author: Ukrit Wattanavaekin
body:
Advice on building a data team, drawn mostly from watching the same mistakes repeat.

## Hiring seniority too late

Three junior analysts without a senior person produce three incompatible definitions of revenue and no way to adjudicate. The first hire sets the conventions everyone else inherits.

## Treating it as a service desk

If the team exists to answer questions, the queue grows forever and the good people leave. The job is to make questions answerable by other people.

## No ownership model

When everyone can build and nobody owns, trust collapses within two quarters. Someone must be accountable for whether a given number is still correct.

## Tooling before definitions

A new warehouse does not resolve a disagreement about what a customer is. The definitions are the work; the tools are how you express them.

## What keeps people

Analysts leave when their work does not change anything. Showing the decision a piece of analysis affected does more for retention than most of the alternatives.

title: Urgent: Upgrade your Metabase installation now. H2-related remote code execution found
excerpt: More vulnerabilities related to H2 connection strings were discovered, and patched. If you are on version 0.43 of Metabase or later, please upgrade IMMEDIATELY.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
An urgent advisory. A remote code execution issue related to H2 database connections has been found. Upgrade immediately.

## Who is affected

Self-hosted instances. If your instance is reachable from the internet, treat this as urgent.

## What to do now

1. Upgrade to a patched version immediately.
2. If you cannot upgrade right now, restrict network access to the instance.
3. Review whether any H2 connections are configured that you do not need.

## Cloud

Already patched. No action required.

A fuller write-up will follow, but it should not delay anyone upgrading.

title: Please upgrade your Metabase immediately
excerpt: We've patched a severe vulnerability uncovered by a third-party security researcher.
author: Sameer Al-Sakran
body:
Please upgrade your Metabase instance immediately. A security issue affecting self-hosted deployments has been patched.

## Action required

Upgrade to the latest patch release of your major version. Cloud instances are already updated.

## If you cannot upgrade today

Restrict network access to the instance. An analytics tool exposed directly to the internet is a larger target than it needs to be, and limiting access reduces exposure to this and to issues not yet discovered.

Details will follow once deployments have had time to update.

title: The two most important business metrics to track
excerpt: Effective metrics are not a one-size-fits-all solution. Here's how to create a useful North Star metric and counter metric to start building out your metrics store.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
If you track two things properly, track these: the rate at which new customers reach value, and the rate at which existing revenue expands or contracts.

## Why these two

Activation tells you whether acquisition is producing anything real. Net revenue retention tells you whether what you built keeps being worth paying for. Between them they cover both ends of the business, and most other metrics are downstream of one or the other.

## Why a metrics store

Because the value is in everyone using the same definition. A metric defined once, centrally, and referenced everywhere is worth more than a better metric defined four times.

## Start small

Two metrics, defined precisely, documented where people will see them. That is more useful than forty in a spreadsheet nobody opens.

title: How to improve data literacy
excerpt: Proven methods and resources to help everyone use data in their everyday tasks.
author: Ukrit Wattanavaekin
body:
Data literacy programmes usually fail because they teach tools rather than scepticism.

## What actually needs teaching

Not how to build a chart. How to ask what a number means, where it came from, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.

## A practical approach

- Teach against your own data, not a sample dataset. People learn when the numbers are about their job.
- Start with reading, not building. Most people need to interpret a dashboard correctly far more often than they need to make one.
- Make definitions visible. Half of data illiteracy is actually undocumented definitions.
- Normalise asking. The person who asks why two reports disagree is doing the organisation a favour.

## The measure

Not course completion. Whether people outside the data team ask better questions six months later.

title: You don't need a data warehouse
excerpt: Start querying your production database as soon as possible, because the best way to model your data warehouse is to prototype it in real life.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
A lot of teams adopt a warehouse before they need one, and pay for it in complexity.

## When you genuinely need one

- Data from several systems that must be joined
- Query load heavy enough to affect your production database
- History your application database does not retain
- Transformations too expensive to run live

## When you do not

If everything lives in one Postgres database, your analytical queries do not disturb production, and you are not retaining years of history — a read replica will take you a long way. Possibly years.

## The actual cost

It is not the bill. It is that every number now has a pipeline between it and the truth, and every pipeline is a thing that breaks silently at 3am.

## The honest version

Many teams should start with a read replica and move when something specific hurts. "We will need it eventually" is not something hurting.

title: The hidden costs of the data stack
excerpt: An incomplete list of the less obvious costs associated with maintaining a data stack, and some things you can do to keep those costs under control.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
The line item is the smallest part of what a data stack costs.

## What the invoice misses

- **Integration time.** Every tool connects to every other tool, and that is where the quarters go.
- **Expertise.** A tool nobody on the team knows well is a tool that produces subtly wrong answers.
- **Latency to an answer.** More layers means longer between a question and a number.
- **Debugging surface.** Each component is somewhere a wrong number can originate.

## The compounding problem

Tools are individually justifiable and collectively unmanageable. Each addition seems small; the combination is a system nobody understands end to end.

## A reasonable test

Before adding a tool, ask who will own it and what gets removed. If the answer to the second is nothing, the stack grows forever.

title: 4 steps to turn your support tickets into an automated dashboard
excerpt: Using Zendesk, Freshdesk, or any other ticketing system? You can start labeling your support tickets for content analysis, and view the results in a support dashboard.
author: Luis Paolini
body:
Support tickets are one of the most under-used datasets in most companies.

## 1. Get them into the warehouse

Most helpdesks have an API or an export. Daily is usually sufficient.

## 2. Categorise

The raw text is not queryable. You need categories — and the useful categorisation is by underlying cause, not by the menu option the customer picked.

## 3. Join to accounts

Tickets in isolation tell you about volume. Tickets joined to account data tell you which customers are struggling, which plans generate support load, and whether ticket rate predicts churn. It usually does.

## 4. Build the dashboard around a decision

Volume by category over time, rate per account, and time to resolution. The actionable chart is categories that are growing, because that is where documentation or a product fix pays off.

## The thing people miss

Ticket rate per account is a leading churn indicator and almost nobody tracks it.

title: How to create and analyze an NPS survey the right way
excerpt: NPS survey data can hold the keys to customer success, but you have to ask the right questions to get the best results.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
NPS is widely used and widely misused. The score is the least interesting output.

## The score is nearly useless alone

A single number compressing a distribution, benchmarked against industries that measure differently. Chasing it as a target produces survey gaming rather than improvement.

## What is useful

- **The free-text responses.** This is the actual data. The score is just how you sort it.
- **The trend within your own business**, same question, same timing, same sampling.
- **Segmentation.** NPS by plan, tenure or support history tells you something. The aggregate does not.

## Running it properly

Ask at a consistent point in the lifecycle. Sample rather than blanketing. Keep it short — the follow-up question matters more than the score, and it is the one people abandon.

## Closing the loop

If a detractor never hears back, you have conducted research rather than improved anything.

title: Automating growth and customer insights in SaaS businesses
excerpt: How a modern data stack can help you improve your customer journey and grow your revenue.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Most growth reporting is assembled by hand each week, which means it is late, inconsistent and nobody fully trusts it.

## What to automate first

The weekly numbers someone currently assembles manually. Not because the analysis is hard, but because doing it by hand guarantees it is inconsistent between weeks and stops entirely when that person is away.

## The pieces

- Signups by source, joined to activation so you can see quality rather than volume
- Cohort retention, updated as cohorts mature
- Expansion and contraction on existing accounts
- Support load per account, as an early warning

## The part that matters

Segment by acquisition source throughout. Two channels with identical cost and different activation rates have very different real costs, and the aggregate hides it completely.

## Then stop

Automating the weekly report frees time for the analysis nobody has done. If it just produces more reports, you have automated the wrong layer.

title: Why interactive embedding?
excerpt: If you want to offer customer analytics, you want interactive embedding.
author: Alexander Kinn
body:
Interactive embedding puts the whole analytical experience inside your application, rather than a fixed dashboard.

## The difference

A static embed shows what you built. Interactive embedding lets your customers ask their own questions — build a query, change a visualisation, save it — inside your product, scoped to their own data.

## When it is worth it

When customers keep asking for reports you did not anticipate. At that point every bespoke report is a maintenance burden, and giving them the tool is cheaper than being the tool.

## What you keep control of

Styling, permissions and scope. They explore their own rows within boundaries you set.

## When it is overkill

If three charts answer everything anyone asks, ship three charts.

title: Bus factor of top GitHub projects
excerpt: What is the bus factor for the top one thousand GitHub repositories with the most stars?
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
The bus factor of a project is how many people would have to disappear before it stalls. We looked at what that number is across widely used open-source projects.

## The method

Attribute commits to contributors, weight by recency since historical contribution does not help with a problem today, then find the smallest group accounting for most of the recent work.

## The finding

It is low. Uncomfortably often it is one. Projects that large numbers of companies depend on frequently have a single person doing most of the current work.

## What it means

Not that these projects are doomed — many have survived for years. But "widely used" is not the same as "well resourced", and the two are frequently confused when people choose dependencies.

## What to do with it

If a dependency is load-bearing for you and has a bus factor of one, that is a risk worth either funding or planning around.

title: Why Metabase Cloud?
excerpt: What you get with Metabase Cloud, and why it's a good deal.
author: Alexander Kinn
body:
Reasons to use the hosted version, and reasons not to.

## The case for

Upgrades, backups and scaling stop being yours. Security patches apply without you noticing. For teams without infrastructure capacity, the maintenance is the entire argument.

## The case against

If you have strict data residency requirements, an existing platform team, or a policy that nothing leaves your network, self-hosting is the right call and the open-source version is fully capable.

## The honest comparison

Self-hosting is not free — it costs someone's attention every month, and that cost is invisible until an upgrade goes wrong. Compare against that rather than against zero.

## Either way

The product is the same. Moving between them is a supported path, not a rewrite.

title: Halloween Edition: Data Horror stories in startups
excerpt: We talked with Amogh Sarda and Ali Baghshomali about common horror data stories in startups and how to avoid them. Read on to learn about the best practices for establishing product events management and upscaling from spreadsheets to the BI.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Real failures, anonymised. Each one happened to someone.

## The dashboard that was wrong for eight months

A join that silently duplicated rows for a subset of customers. Revenue overstated. Found when an invoice disagreed with the dashboard.

## The metric with four definitions

Four teams, four numbers, one board meeting. Discovered live.

## The pipeline nobody owned

It broke on a Friday. Nobody noticed until Tuesday, because the dashboard showed the last successful run and looked completely normal.

## The timezone

Daily numbers computed in UTC, targets set in local time. Every month-end was wrong by one day's trading, consistently, for a year.

## The common thread

None of these were visibly broken. They all produced plausible numbers. The failure mode that matters is not the error — it is the error that looks fine.

title: The data guide to travel
excerpt: We scraped some data from Google Maps to find out what the top attractions are in the world’s most visited destinations.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
An exploration of public travel data: when to book, where prices actually vary, and which conventional wisdom survives contact with the numbers.

## Booking windows

The advice about an optimal number of weeks ahead is roughly right on average and useless in particular. Variance within a route is far larger than the difference between booking windows.

## Day of week

The effect exists and is smaller than commonly claimed. Route and season dominate.

## What actually predicts price

Competition on the route. Routes with one operator are expensive regardless of when you book; routes with three are cheaper at almost any point.

## The methodological caveat

This is observational data with obvious selection effects. Prices observed are prices offered, not prices paid, and that gap is not random.

title: How Metabase uses Metabase
excerpt: Here at Metabase, we use Metabase internally, so we thought it'd be fun to use Metabase to see how we use Metabase.
author: Jeff Bruemmer
body:
We run our own company on our own product. Here is what that actually looks like, including the parts that are not flattering.

## What we track

Instance telemetry where people have opted in, support load, sales pipeline, and the open-source community — issues, contributions, release adoption.

## The dashboards that matter

Fewer than you would expect. A handful get opened daily; the rest were built for a moment and survive out of inertia. We run the same housekeeping we recommend, and we are not better at it than anyone else.

## Dogfooding problems

Using your own product daily makes you fast at it, which makes you a bad judge of how hard it is for a newcomer. The features that frustrate us are rarely the ones that frustrate new users.

## The useful habit

Every team maintains its own collection rather than filing requests with a central group. That is the thing most worth copying.

title: Want to retire early? Save more money
excerpt: Japan and Korea’s high average savings rates drive shorter times to reach financial independence.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
An exploration of early retirement arithmetic, where the conclusion is less interesting than the sensitivity.

## The model

Savings rate, expected return, withdrawal rate. The headline result — that savings rate dominates — is well known and holds up.

## What the charts show

The relationship is sharply non-linear. Moving from a 10% to a 20% savings rate removes far more years than moving from 50% to 60%. Most of the available gain is at the low end.

## Where it gets fragile

The withdrawal rate assumption carries almost all the uncertainty. Small changes there swing the answer by a decade, which is worth knowing before treating any particular number as a plan.

## The honest caveat

This is arithmetic, not advice. The model assumes stable returns and stable spending, and reality supplies neither.

title: #jobs #jobs #jobs | Exploring trends in data jobs postings
excerpt: Building a dashboard using data from the dbt Slack to analyze how data jobs have been changing over time.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
An analysis of data job postings — what titles exist, what they ask for, and how little the two correlate.

## Titles are noise

"Data analyst", "analytics engineer" and "BI developer" describe overlapping work with no consistency between companies. The same responsibilities appear under all three, and the same title covers wildly different jobs.

## What the requirements actually say

SQL is near-universal. Python appears in most postings and is genuinely required in fewer. The tooling lists are long and largely aspirational — a posting naming nine tools is describing a wish, not a filter.

## The signal worth reading

Whether the posting describes outcomes or tools. Postings that describe what the person will change tend to come from organisations that have thought about why the role exists.

## For candidates

Read the responsibilities, ignore the title, and treat the tool list as negotiable.

title: Building a better data culture for your team
excerpt: What are the best ways to build a data-centric culture within an organization? TJ Muehleman and Krishnan Raghupathi are sharing their experience and advice on how to get started.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Data culture is one of those phrases that means nothing until you define it as a set of behaviours.

## What it looks like in practice

- People check a number before asserting it in a meeting
- Disagreeing with a dashboard is normal rather than rude
- Definitions are written down and referenced
- Somebody owns each important number

## How it fails

Usually through one bad experience. Someone brings data to a meeting, the number is questioned, nobody can resolve it, and the lesson learned is that bringing data is risky. That happens twice and people stop.

## What helps

Make it easy to check. If the definition is next to the number and the query is one click away, a disagreement takes two minutes rather than a week.

## The leadership part

If leaders use data selectively — citing it when it agrees and dismissing it when it does not — everyone notices, and no amount of tooling compensates.

title: A product manager's guide to getting started with Metabase
excerpt: You may have plenty of product management tools at your disposal, but really getting to know your product data and customers is still a challenge. Learn how Metabase can help your product team make smarter data-driven decisions without relying exclusively on event instrumentation.
author: Tanya Aulachynskaya
body:
A short orientation for product managers, written around the questions PMs actually ask.

## Start with one question

Not a dashboard. One specific question — how many accounts used the feature we shipped last month, and did they come back. Answering it teaches you the tool faster than any tour.

## The three things worth learning

- **The query builder**, enough to filter and group without help
- **Drill-through**, because the follow-up question is always "which ones?"
- **Saved questions as a starting point**, so you build on the data team's work rather than starting from raw tables

## What to ask your data team for

A model covering your product's core events with sensible column names. One good model is worth more than ten dashboards.

## The habit to build

After every launch, look. Most feature usage questions never get asked because nobody made it a routine.

title: A marketer's guide to getting started with Metabase
excerpt: Your marketing team moves fast, and doesn't have the time to spend weeks vetting and configuring an analytics tool. Learn how Metabase can help you level up those growth initiatives.
author: Alexander Kinn
body:
An orientation for marketers who want to stop waiting on an analyst for channel performance.

## The question you actually have

Not how many clicks. Which channels send people who stay. That requires joining campaign data to product usage, and that join is the whole reason this matters.

## What to learn first

Filtering and grouping a saved question. If your data team has modelled signups with an acquisition source, you can answer most channel questions from there without writing SQL.

## The metric that changes decisions

Activation rate by source. Two channels with the same cost per signup and different activation rates have completely different real costs, and the aggregate spend report hides it entirely.

## Working with the data team

Ask for a model, not a dashboard. A dashboard answers this week's question; a model lets you answer next week's yourself.

title: Maintaining healthy skepticism toward your data
excerpt: Your data isn't infallible, but it takes practice to get comfortable interrogating that data when you get an unexpected result. Learn how you can hone your data intuition and keep cool in the face of fluctuating numbers.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
The most useful analytical habit is assuming the number is wrong until you have a reason to think otherwise.

## Why

Because the failure mode that costs you is not the obviously broken dashboard. It is the plausible number that is quietly incorrect, which nobody questions precisely because it looks reasonable.

## Questions worth asking every time

- Does the row count make sense, or did a join multiply something?
- What happens at the boundaries — timezone, month end, null handling?
- Does this agree with a number from a different system?
- If this were wrong, how would I find out?

## The cross-check

Reconciling against something independent — an invoice, a vendor dashboard, a manual count — catches more real errors than any amount of staring at SQL.

## Scepticism is not cynicism

The goal is a number you can defend, not a reason to ignore all numbers.

title: Your chart has too many series: data visualization tips for the non-analyst
excerpt: Creating effective charts and dashboards isn't always intuitive for those outside the analyst bubble. We've pulled together some tips to help you make sure your data visualizations are the best they can be.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Advice for non-analysts who have to make charts, starting with the most common problem.

## Your chart has too many series

Seven lines is not a chart, it is a legend with decoration. Three or four is the practical limit. If you need more, use small multiples — several small charts sharing an axis, which people read far more easily than one crowded one.

## Other frequent ones

- **Truncated axes on bar charts.** Bar length is the encoding; truncating it misleads.
- **Rainbow colour schemes** where the colours mean nothing.
- **Pie charts with eight slices.** Two or three is fine. Eight is unreadable.
- **Dual axes**, which can be made to show almost any relationship you want.

## The test

Show it to someone who was not in the meeting and ask what it says. If they hesitate, the chart is not finished.

title: Calculating LTV: are you doing it wrong?
excerpt: You've heard that customer lifetime value (LTV) is an important metric, but how exactly are you supposed to know what formula to use? This article offers a simple LTV formula for SaaS companies, along with use cases for the metrics and common pitfalls people encounter when working with LTV.
author: Bruno Bergher
body:
Lifetime value is one of the most confidently miscalculated numbers in business.

## The usual mistake

Average revenue divided by churn rate, on the whole customer base. This is wrong in several ways at once: it averages over segments that behave completely differently, assumes churn is constant when it is highest early, and uses revenue rather than margin.

## What to do instead

- Calculate by cohort and segment, never in aggregate
- Use contribution margin, not revenue
- Use observed retention curves rather than a flat churn assumption
- Discount future revenue; money in year three is not money today

## The honest version

For a young company, LTV is largely a projection. Quoting it to two decimal places implies a confidence the data does not support.

## What it is useful for

Comparing segments and channels against each other. Much less useful as an absolute number.

title: Metabase is SOC 2 Type 1 Compliant
excerpt: Metabase has always cared about data privacy, and today we’re proud to announce we're now SOC 2 Type 1 compliant.
author: Alexander Kinn
body:
Metabase has completed a SOC 2 Type 1 audit.

## What it covers

An independent assessment that our security controls are designed appropriately as of the audit date — access control, change management, encryption, incident response and vendor management.

## What Type 1 means

It assesses design at a point in time. Type 2 assesses operating effectiveness over a period, and that is the next step.

## Why we did it

Because security review is a real part of adopting an analytics tool, and completing the audit saves customers from reconstructing the answers themselves.

## Getting the report

Available under NDA through our team.

title: The perfect chart: choosing the right visualization for every scenario
excerpt: Data viz is all about communicating the right story. Line charts are a reliable standby, but it's good to have options. Read on for tips and examples about when to use scatterplots, progress bars, and more.
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
A practical guide to picking a chart, organised by the question rather than the chart type.

## Match the question

- **Comparing categories** → bar chart, sorted by value
- **Change over time** → line chart
- **Part of a whole** → stacked bar, or a pie only with two or three slices
- **Relationship between two measures** → scatter plot
- **A single important number** → just show the number, large
- **Finding a specific value** → a table, which is frequently the correct answer

## The most common error

Choosing for visual interest rather than for the question. A table is often the right answer and rarely the chosen one.

## Distribution

Underused. If you are showing an average, a histogram usually tells a more honest story — averages hide bimodality completely.

## The rule underneath

The chart should make the answer obvious without a paragraph of explanation.

title: Avoiding analyst burnout: how to streamline ad hoc requests
excerpt: Help your analysts avoid burnout with these tips for handling ad hoc analysis requests (hint: the answer lies in self-service analytics!).
author: Margaret Rimek
body:
Ad hoc requests are the main cause of analyst burnout, and adding analysts does not fix it.

## Why the queue regenerates

Most requests are variations on something already answered, from people who could not find the previous answer or could not tell whether it was still valid. That is discoverability, not capacity.

## What actually reduces it

- A searchable place where answered questions live, findable using the words a non-analyst would use
- Models that make common questions answerable without a join
- Visible ownership, so stale work has someone to ask
- Tickets rather than Slack messages, so patterns become visible

## Train one person per team

Not everyone needs to self-serve. One capable person per department handles most of their team's questions and knows when to escalate.

## The trade-off

Documenting a request so the next person self-serves takes three times as long as answering it. It only pays if you do it consistently, which is why it usually does not happen.

title: Business intelligence career paths
excerpt: To the uninitiated, BI career paths may sound a lot alike. We've written up an explainer on the difference between the following common roles within data teams: data analyst, data scientist, BI developer, data engineer, and analytics engineer.
author: Jess Thompson
body:
Business intelligence does not have one career path, which is confusing when you are early in it.

## The directions people go

- **Deeper technical** — analytics engineering, data modelling, infrastructure
- **Domain specialist** — becoming the person who understands the business, not just the data
- **Management** — leading a data team, which is a different job rather than a promotion
- **Adjacent product roles** — data-heavy product or growth work

## What transfers

SQL transfers. Tool expertise transfers less than people hope. The skill that transfers most is translating a vague question into a specific answerable one, and it is the hardest to demonstrate on a CV.

## Choosing

The useful question is not which pays more. It is whether you would rather go deeper into systems or deeper into a business. Both are legitimate and the people who are unhappy are usually the ones who drifted rather than chose.

## The practical advice

Keep a record of decisions your analysis changed. It is more persuasive than a list of tools, and almost nobody does it.
